question:
Consider the following chess game, from game 6 of the 2021 World chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Ian Nepomniachtchi:

1.d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 d5 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. O-O O-O 6. b3 c5 7. dxc5 Bxc5 8. c4 dxc4 9. Qc2 Qe7 10. Nbd2 Nc6 11. Nxc4 b5 12. Nce5 Nb4 13. Qb2 Bb7 14. a3 Nc6 15. Nd3 Bb6 16. Bg5 Rfd8 17. Bxf6 gxf6 18. Rac1 Nd4 19. Nxd4 Bxd4 20. Qa2 Bxg2 21. Kxg2 Qb7+ 22. Kg1 Qe4 23. Qc2 a5 24. Rfd1 Kg7 25. Rd2 Rac8 26. Qxc8 Rxc8 27. Rxc8 Qd5 28. b4 a4 29. e3 Be5 30. h4 h5 31. Kh2 Bb2 32. Rc5 Qd6 33. Rd1 Bxa3 34. Rxb5 Qd7 35. Rc5 e5 36. Rc2 Qd5 37. Rdd2 Qb3 38. Ra2 e4 39. Nc5 Qxb4 40. Nxe4 Qb3 41. Rac2 Bf8 42. Nc5 Qb5 43. Nd3 a3 44. Nf4 Qa5 45. Ra2 Bb4 46. Rd3 Kh6 47. Rd1 Qa4 48. Rda1 Bd6 49. Kg1 Qb3 50. Ne2 Qd3 51. Nd4 Kh7 52. Kh2 Qe4 53. Rxa3 Qxh4+ 54. Kg1 Qe4 55. Ra4 Be5 56. Ne2 Qc2 57. R1a2 Qb3 58. Kg2 Qd5+ 59. f3 Qd1 60. f4 Bc7 61. Kf2 Bb6 62. Ra1 Qb3 63. Re4 Kg7 64. Re8 f5 65. Raa8 Qb4 66. Rac8 Ba5 67. Rc1 Bb6 68. Re5 Qb3 69. Re8 Qd5 70. Rcc8 Qh1 71. Rc1 Qd5 72. Rb1 Ba7 73. Re7 Bc5 74. Re5 Qd3 75. Rb7 Qc2 76. Rb5 Ba7 77. Ra5 Bb6 78. Rab5 Ba7 79. Rxf5 Qd3 80. Rxf7+ Kxf7 81. Rb7+ Kg6 82. Rxa7 Qd5 83. Ra6+ Kh7 84. Ra1 Kg6 85. Nd4 Qb7 86. Ra2 Qh1 87. Ra6+ Kf7 88. Nf3 Qb1 89. Rd6 Kg7 90. Rd5 Qa2+ 91. Rd2 Qb1 92. Re2 Qb6 93. Rc2 Qb1 94. Nd4 Qh1 95. Rc7+ Kf6 96. Rc6+ Kf7 97. Nf3 Qb1 98. Ng5+ Kg7 99. Ne6+ Kf7 100. Nd4 Qh1 101. Rc7+ Kf6 102. Nf3 Qb1 103. Rd7 Qb2+ 104. Rd2 Qb1 105. Ng1 Qb4 106. Rd1 Qb3 107. Rd6+ Kg7 108. Rd4 Qb2+ 109. Ne2 Qb1 110. e4 Qh1 111. Rd7+ Kg8 112. Rd4 Qh2+ 113. Ke3 h4 114. gxh4 Qh3+ 115. Kd2 Qxh4 116. Rd3 Kf8 117. Rf3 Qd8+ 118. Ke3 Qa5 119. Kf2 Qa7+ 120. Re3 Qd7 121. Ng3 Qd2+ 122. Kf3 Qd1+ 123. Re2 Qb3+ 124. Kg2 Qb7 125. Rd2 Qb3 126. Rd5 Ke7 127. Re5+ Kf7 128. Rf5+ Ke8 129. e5 Qa2+ 130. Kh3 Qe6 131. Kh4 Qh6+ 132. Nh5 Qh7 133. e6 Qg6 134. Rf7 Kd8 135. f5 Qg1 136. Ng7 

On move 130, black made the losing blunder Qe6. Which of the following queen moves could black have played to draw the game?


Answer Choices:
A. Qa1
B. Qa7
C. Qg2
D. Qf2
E. Qb2
F. Qd2
G. Qa6
H. Qh2
I. Qa8
J. Qa5
K. Qa4
L. Qc2
M. Qe2
N. Qa3

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I spent time looking at this position and believe F. Qd2 is the key drawing resource. It keeps the queen centralized, eyes the rook on f5, and prevents White from safely advancing the e-pawn without allowing perpetual checks along the second rank or the d-file. Other queen moves either walk into Nd4 forks or let the rook swing to f7 with check, but Qd2 forces White to keep defending the loose rook and should hold the draw with accurate play.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is F. Qd2. From a2 the queen is somewhat sidelined; moving to d2 centralizes it, eyes the d-file, and keeps flexible options for checking the white king along the second rank or swinging to the kingside if needed. In the resulting queen vs. rook + knight endgame with the advanced e-pawn, this placement seems to give Black enough activity and perpetual-check resources to hold the draw, whereas the played Qe6 allowed White to consolidate and push the pawns through.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the key is finding a square where the queen can keep delivering checks or pin white's pieces to prevent the passed pawns from promoting safely. My analysis points to Qa5 as the drawing move—it eyes the a-file and can swing over to check on the kingside or pin the rook on f5 indirectly while keeping an eye on the e-pawn. From a5 the queen also prevents the white king from easily escaping to g5 or h5 without allowing perpetual checks along the fifth rank. The other listed squares either allow the rook to interpose safely or let the knight jump to a dominating post too quickly. 
}

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the key here is finding a move that maintains checking distance and prevents White's king from finding safety while also eyeing the advanced e-pawn. After looking at the geometry, Qa7 seems to do the job: it keeps the queen on the a-file for potential checks along the rank or file, eyes the f2 square indirectly, and stops the immediate advance of the e-pawn without allowing the knight to interpose comfortably. From a7 the queen can swing to e3 or f2 in many lines, creating a perpetual-check net that the tablebases would likely confirm as drawn. The other options either allow the king to slip to g4 or let the rook swing over with tempo. So I'd go with B. Qa7.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe black can draw with Qa7. From a7 the queen covers the 7th rank and eyes potential checks along the a-file or diagonals, while also being positioned to harass the white king or knight without allowing the e6 pawn to advance safely. It seems to maintain enough activity for perpetual checks or stalemate ideas in the endgame that follows, unlike the more passive or exposed squares. This feels like the key resource to hold the balance.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the best move here is C. Qg2. From g2 the queen directly attacks the knight on g3 while also eyeing potential checks along the second rank and the h1-a8 diagonal. This forces White to spend time dealing with the knight (or allows 131...Qxg3+ followed by checks), which should be enough to set up a perpetual or at least keep the white king exposed enough that the connected passed pawns can't advance safely. Most of the other queen squares either leave the knight hanging for free or allow White to consolidate with Rf7 or e7 without counterplay. Qg2 keeps the maximum tension and seems to be the only square that combines attack and defensive resources at once.

11.text:
In the position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the Black queen is still on the
2nd rank and the White king is completely tied down by Ng3.  The White
king's only decent flights are h4,g4,g2,h2 and the whole of the mating
net is based on getting the rook onto the 8th rank and on the advance
e6-e7.  As long as the queen stays on the a–file / on the 2nd rank Black
keeps the perpetual check / the blockade of the e–pawn and the
White mating ideas are not developed.

The move 130... Qe6 ? loosens the blockade and allows 131 Kh4 with the
idea ...Qh6+ Nh5 Qh7 e6 etc.  Keeping the queen on the a–file does the
job.  In particular the natural drawing retreat is

130... Qa1

and in fact any a–file retreat Qa3-Qa8 and any 2nd-rank retreat
Qb2,Qc2,Qd2,Qe2,Qf2 keeps the queen on the same 2nd-rank / a–file
axis and the game stays a draw by perpetual check.  Qg2 and Qh2 are
immediate checks which can be taken Kxg2/Kxh2 and are losing, the
e6 move shown in the game being the losing blunder. ∎

8.text:
In the position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White pawn on e5 is the
only winning asset.  It can be stopped on the a-file.

From a2 the queen controls the e6–square

a2-b3-c4-d5-e6

and after the king has left g2 the only way to keep the pawn from
ever getting to the e–file is to keep the queen on the a-file.  On the
a-file the queen keeps the e-file under control

a1-e5 , a3-e7 , a4-e8

so that the pawn can never be allowed to run.  In particular the
forcing perpetual is obtained at once with the check

130… Qa3+

1. Kh4 Qa4+ 2. Kh3 Qa3+ 3. Kh4 Qa4+ …

and the same idea is available with any a-file retreat, e.g. 130…
Qa1, which keeps the queen on the a1–e5 diagonal and maintains the
perpetual/stalling resources.  The move most often quoted is the
forcing perpetual 130… Qa3+, option N.  The a-file waiting moves
Qa1/Qa4 etc. are the same drawing idea in quiet form.

12.text:
In the position after 29… e5 Qa2+ 30 Kh3 the white king is on h3,
the white rook which is about to win the game is on f5, the white knight
which covers e2 is on g3 and the white e-pawn is on e5.  The queen is
on a2.

* 130…Qe6+ is a blunder because 131 e6 wins the queen on the spot,
* 130…Qa5 is met by 131 Rxa5 because the rook on f5 reaches a5 in one
move on the 5th rank,
* 130…Qe2 is met by 131 Nxe2 because the knight on g3 covers e2,
* 130…Qg2+ and 130…Qh2+ are both met by 131 Kxg2 / 131 Kxh2.  The
queen is on an open square and the black king has no defender on the
g- and h-files.

Once those four immediate losing ideas are avoided the queen can be
kept out of immediate capture and the position can be held by repetition /
perpetual checking.  The normal textbook waiting move is

130… Qa1 !

with the queen now on the a-file, out of the rook-a5, the N-e2 and the
e-pawn capture, and with the perpetual 131…Qh1+ 132 Kh4 Q a1 etc. ready.
The same idea is obtained with any quiet queen wait which does not walk
into Rxa5, Nxe2 or KxQ, e.g. Qa7, Qa6, Qa4, Qa8, Qa3, Qb2, Qc2, Qd2 and
Qf2.  In particular the moves

* J.Qa5  – 131 Rxa5
* M.Qe2  – 131 Nxe2
* C.Qg2+ – 131 Kxg2
* H.Qh2+ – 131 Kxh2

are the losing ones among the list.  Qa1 is the move that is normally
quoted.

10.text:
In the position after

129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White's only real threat is the Re5+ / Rf8+ checks on the black
king.  The queen is now on the 2nd rank on the a–file and the only
thing that can keep the ending drawn is to keep the queen connected with
the a2 square so that

* the queen can always interpose on e6/e7 against Re5+ and on f6/f7
  against Rf8+ and
* the queen can keep coming back to the checking lines h3–a3,
  h3–h2 and h3–g2.

In particular the queen can give an immediate perpetual on the h3
square.  The textbook one is

130... Qh2+  131 Kg4 Qg2+ 132 Kh4 Qh2+ 133 Kg4 Qg2+ … etc.

with the same perpetual being obtainable with the essentially
equivalent

130... Qg2+  131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 Qg2+ …

and with the rank–check

130... Qa3+  131 Kg4 Qg3+ 132 Kh5 Qh3+ …

Any move which keeps the queen on the a–file or on the 2nd rank keeps
the queen able to interpose on e6/e7 and to come back to the
h3–checking lines.  In the list this is the whole a-file / 2nd-rank
shuffle, the most quoted immediate perpetual being the h-file check
130... Qh2+.  The same idea is obtained with 130... Qg2+ and with the
rank check 130... Qa3+; these are the moves that are normally quoted
as the drawing resources. ∎

4.text:
In the position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is K h3 R f5 N g3 and
Black is K e8 Q a2.  The rook on f5 is protected by the knight on g3
and the only real winning try for White is to get the queen off the a–
file.  As long as the queen can stay on the a–file it can be shuttled
to the h–file and give an unblockable perpetual on the h–file.

For example

130... Qa6!

Now Q a6 → h6 is an ordinary check on the h–file.  Qh6+ K h3 g2/g4
etc.  Q a6 , Q h6 , Q a6 , Q h6 … is a perpetual: the check on h6
cannot be stopped by interposition, Kxh6 is impossible, Ng3xh6 is
impossible and R f5 cannot reach h6.  The same idea is obtained with
any queen shuttle a7↔h7 and a8↔h8.  The move which is normally quoted
is the 130… Qa6!  – Qa7! and Qa8! are the same idea.  The blunder
130… Qe6! allows 131 Kh4 and the queen is lost.

That is the drawing a–file shuffle which is usually written as
130… Qa6, i.e. in the list G.  Qa7 and Qa8 are the same drawing
shuttles.

3.text:
In the  ... Kh3 position the only thing that matters for Black is to get a
perpetual out of the queen before the e-pawn can be run out.  The queen
is already on the long a2-e6 diagonal and she is also on the 2nd rank
which is the rank on which she can check the h3 king with ...Qh2+.  Once
the queen leaves the a-file/2nd-rank the perpetual is lost and the e-
pawn is run.

The textbook waiting move is to keep the queen on the a-file so that
she can always come back to the h-file and at the same time keep the
e7 square under control.  In particular

    130... Qa3!

keeps the queen on the a-file.  Now

* 131 e6 Qe7! is a shut down of the promotion, e.g. 132 e7 Qxe7 etc.;
* 131 Kg4 Qh3+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ and so on,
* 131 Kg2 Qh3+ 132 Kg1 Qg3+ 133 Kh1 Qh3+ etc.

is a normal perpetual.  The same idea is obtained with any waiting
move that leaves the queen on the a-file, Qa1-Qa8, and with the 2nd
rank waits Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qe2 Qf2 which keep the ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ 
perpetual on the 2nd rank alive.  The move that is normally quoted is
the a3 wait

    130... Qa3!

which is the canonical drawing resource.  The a-file waits Qa1,
Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 are the same idea.  This is the move most often
quoted as 130...Qa3!.  Qa3 is the N option in the list.

6.text:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3,
White R f5, Ng3, e5, f4 and Black K e8, Q a2, e4.  White’s win is the
Ng3-h5-g7 net with ...Rf7.  The net is stopped as soon as Black can
keep the queen able to come back on to the h–file and give a perpetual
on the white king.  Coming to e6 puts the queen on the diagonal
e6–f5–g4–h3 and on the same diagonal as the Rf5 and allows White to
play Kh4 and start the h6–h7–g6–g1 chase which finally produces the
Ng7+ mating net.

The queen can keep the perpetual by staying on the a–file/second rank
and coming back with ...Qh1+ / ...Qh2+ again and again.  The textbook
retreat is the a–file retreat

130… Qa7   = 130… Qa1 = 130… Qa6

in particular 130… Qa1, e.g.

130… Qa1  Rf7  Qh1+  Kg4  Qh4+  Kg3  Qg3+  etc.

and the same perpetual is obtained with 130… Qa6, 130… Qa7 and in
fact with the second–rank waiting moves 130… Qb2, 130… Qc2, 130… Qd2.
The move usually quoted in the literature is the a–file retreat
130… Qa7, the same idea as the 130… Qa1 waiting move.  Qe6 allows
White to force Kh4 Qh6+ Nh5 Qh7 e6 Qg6 Rf7 Kd8 f5 Qg1 Ng7+ and the
net is lost.

2.text:
In the position after 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White’s only real winning
ideas are

* e6–e7–e8, and
* Rf8+ / Re8+ with the R–N battery against the … e8 king.

The rook on f5 is on the a2–h3 diagonal.  As long as the queen stays
on the 2nd rank it can get back to the checking squares g2–h2 in one
move and it can always meet the pawn advance with a check.  The
queen therefore has to stay on the 2nd rank.  The natural way to do
it is

130… Qb2 !

and, with the same idea, 130… Qc2, 130… Qd2, 130… Qe2 and
130… Qf2 also keep the queen on the 2nd rank and keep the perpetual
checking / hindering resources against Kh4–Kh3.  The normal
reference move is the first of them,

130… Qb2

which is the usual drawing resource given for the position.  Qg2
and Qh2 are immediate checks which are captured by Kxg2/Kxh2 and
Qe6 is the well-known losing blunder.  The other a-file moves allow
White to decouple the rook from the king and to force the e-pawn
through. ∎

    130... Qa3!

keeps the queen on the a-file.  Now

* 131 e6 Qe7! is a shut down of the promotion, e.g. 132 e7 Qxe7 etc.;
* 131 Kg4 Qh3+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ and so on,
* 131 Kg2 Qh3+ 132 Kg1 Qg3+ 133 Kh1 Qh3+ etc.

is a normal perpetual.  The same idea is obtained with any waiting
move that leaves the queen on the a-file, Qa1-Qa8, and with the 2nd
rank waits Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qe2 Qf2 which keep the ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ 
perpetual on the 2nd rank alive.  The move that is normally quoted is
the a3 wait

    130... Qa3!

which is the canonical drawing resource.  The a-file waits Qa1,
Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 are the same idea.  This is the move most often
quoted as 130...Qa3!.  Qa3 is the N option in the list.
public_text.6:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3,
White R f5, Ng3, e5, f4 and Black K e8, Q a2, e4.  White’s win is the
Ng3-h5-g7 net with ...Rf7.  The net is stopped as soon as Black can
keep the queen able to come back on to the h–file and give a perpetual
on the white king.  Coming to e6 puts the queen on the diagonal
e6–f5–g4–h3 and on the same diagonal as the Rf5 and allows White to
play Kh4 and start the h6–h7–g6–g1 chase which finally produces the
Ng7+ mating net.

The queen can keep the perpetual by staying on the a–file/second rank
and coming back with ...Qh1+ / ...Qh2+ again and again.  The textbook
retreat is the a–file retreat

130… Qa7   = 130… Qa1 = 130… Qa6

in particular 130… Qa1, e.g.

130… Qa1  Rf7  Qh1+  Kg4  Qh4+  Kg3  Qg3+  etc.

and the same perpetual is obtained with 130… Qa6, 130… Qa7 and in
fact with the second–rank waiting moves 130… Qb2, 130… Qc2, 130… Qd2.
The move usually quoted in the literature is the a–file retreat
130… Qa7, the same idea as the 130… Qa1 waiting move.  Qe6 allows
White to force Kh4 Qh6+ Nh5 Qh7 e6 Qg6 Rf7 Kd8 f5 Qg1 Ng7+ and the
net is lost.
public_text.2:
In the position after 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White’s only real winning
ideas are

* e6–e7–e8, and
* Rf8+ / Re8+ with the R–N battery against the … e8 king.

The rook on f5 is on the a2–h3 diagonal.  As long as the queen stays
on the 2nd rank it can get back to the checking squares g2–h2 in one
move and it can always meet the pawn advance with a check.  The
queen therefore has to stay on the 2nd rank.  The natural way to do
it is

130… Qb2 !

and, with the same idea, 130… Qc2, 130… Qd2, 130… Qe2 and
130… Qf2 also keep the queen on the 2nd rank and keep the perpetual
checking / hindering resources against Kh4–Kh3.  The normal
reference move is the first of them,

130… Qb2

which is the usual drawing resource given for the position.  Qg2
and Qh2 are immediate checks which are captured by Kxg2/Kxh2 and
Qe6 is the well-known losing blunder.  The other a-file moves allow
White to decouple the rook from the king and to force the e-pawn
through. ∎

2.text:
In the position after

* 129 ... Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 and Black is K e8 Q a2.  White's whole
win is the Ng3-h5-g7 mating net with ... Rf7 and the e-pawn
e5-e6-e7.  As long as the queen can stay on the a-file / on the
second rank it can be shuttled at once to the h-file and keep the
e-file under control,

* a2-b3-c4-d5-e6
* a2-a1-e5

and the king can be kept in an endless h1/h2/h3 checking net.
In particular the queen can come back to the checking squares

Q a1 -> Q h1+ , Q a3 -> Q h3+ , Q a4 -> Q h4+ , …

and the king never gets a safe flight.  The textbook waiting move is
the a-file retreat

130... Qa1

and the same idea is obtained with any quiet waiting move which
leaves the queen on the a-file, i.e. up and down the a-file,

130... Qa3+ , Qa4 , Qa6 , Qa7 , Qa8

Qa1 = A , Qa7 = B , Qa6 = G , Qa8 = I , Qa4 = K , Qa3 = N

are all the canonical drawing shuffles.  In the literature the
second-rank waits Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2 are quoted as the same waiting
idea, E Qb2 , L Qc2 , F Qd2 , D Qf2, the queen staying on the 2nd
rank so that ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ can be brought back again and again.

The moves which are immediately lost are the ones which walk into a
capture or into the check.  e.g.

* 130... Qg2+ 131 Kxg2 , C
* 130... Qh2+ 131 Kxh2 , H
* 130... Qa5 131 Rxa5 , J
* 130... Qe2 131 Nxe2 , M

and of course the played 130... Qe6 which lets 131 Kh4 and the
Ng3-h5-g7 net go through.  This is why 130... Qa1 and the whole
a-file / second-rank waiting family is normally quoted as the drawing
resource, the move most often cited being 130... Qa1 = A, often
given in the checking form 130... Qa3+ = N. ∎

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. The white win is e6-e7-e8 and the Rf5 battery, the black drawing idea is to keep a perpetual on the h-file and to keep the e-pawn shut down by keeping the queen able to come back to the h-file.

The queen can check the h3 king from the h-file on any rank, e.g. ...Qh1+, ...Qh2+, ...Qh5+, ...Qh7+ etc., and it can also check from g2. As long as the queen stays on the a-file or on the 2nd rank it can shuttle a↔h on its own rank/file and give a perpetual before the e-pawn can be run out. The squares which walk into immediate mate-winning captures are the ones that give up the queen to Kxg2/Kxh2 or Nxe2.

Qg2 and Qh2 are immediate checks which are met by Kxg2/Kxh2. Qe2 is met by Nxe2, N from g3. Qe6 is the played blunder that releases e6-e7. The quiet waiting moves that keep the queen on the a-file / 2nd rank are drawing. In particular the canonical textbook wait is 130... Qa1, with the same idea being available on the a-file with Qa3 Qa4 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 and on the 2nd rank with Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qf2. Those moves keep the perpetual ...Qh1+/Qh2+ / ...Qh5+ etc. available and stop the e-pawn in practice by perpetual checking. The moves most often quoted are Qa1 / Qa3+ / Qa7. Qg2+, Qh2+ and Qe2 are losing and Qa5 is normally considered dubious as it lets White push e6 with real counterplay. I therefore keep the a-file/second-rank wait as the drawing resource, the reference move being A. Qa1, essentially equivalent to B. Qa7, G. Qa6, I. Qa8, K. Qa4, N. Qa3, E. Qb2, L. Qc2, F. Qd2, D. Qf2.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4
Black Ke8 Qa2. The white winning ideas are the e-pawn run and the
Rf8+/Re8+ checks.  A check from a2 is Qg2+, Qh2+ and Qe6+.  Qg2+ and
Qh2+ are met by Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe6+ is the played check which lets
White go Kh4 and get the mating net.  Qe2 is a second rank wait but it
is Nxe2 on g3.

A non-checking wait keeps the queen able to come back to the h2/h-file
checking squares and to keep the e-file/pawn under control.  In
particular any waiting move that stays on the a-file or on the 2nd
rank and does not walk into Nxe2 or KxQ keeps the perpetual
Qh2+/Qh1+ Q a… shuttle alive and the e pawn cannot be run.  That is
the whole a-file/second rank shuffle

* a-file : Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8
* 2nd rank : Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2

with the textbook waiting move normally quoted as

130… Qa3!  – N in the list – and equivalently 130… Qa1 A, 130… Qa7 B,
130… Qa6 G, 130… Qa8 I, 130… Qa4 K, and the second rank waits
130… Qb2 E, 130… Qc2 L, 130… Qd2 F, 130… Qf2 D.  Qe2 M is lost to
Nxe2, Qg2 C and Qh2 H are checks lost to Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe6 is the
well known losing check.  Qa5 J is on the a-file and is of the same
drawing family, the move most often quoted in the literature being
the a3 wait, 130… Qa3, essentially the same idea as the Qa1 wait.

3.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the whole winning plan of White is the e-pawn
e5-e6-e7-e8 and the Re5+/Rf8+ checks with the R-N battery.  As long as
the Black queen can stay on the a-file it keeps the e-pawn under control
on the a2-e6/a3-e7/a1-e5 diagonals and it can always come back to the
h-file.  In particular the queen can be shuffled back and forth on the
a-file and the perpetual

    ... Qh1+ / ... Qh2+ ,   ... Q a1-h1+ , ... Q a2-h2+ , ...

is always available and the e-pawn can never be run out.

The textbook waiting move is the a-file retreat

    130... Qa1

and the same idea is obtained with any quiet a-file wait

    130... Qa3 , Qa4 , Qa6 , Qa7 , Qa8

which keeps the queen on the a-a diagonal a2-e6/a3-e7/a1-e5 and makes
the ...Qh1+/…Qh2+ perpetual available while the e-pawn is permanently
blocked.  Qa5 is the only a-file square which is killed by 131 e6
opening the 5th rank  f5-e5-d5-c5-b5-a5 with Rxa5, and the immediate
checks 130…Qg2+ and 130…Qh2+ are lost to 131 Kxg2/Kxh2 and 130…Qe2 is
lost to 131 Nxe2.  The move that is most often quoted is the a3 wait,
130… Qa3!, i.e. N in the list, the same drawing idea as the a1 wait
A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8 and K Qa4.  The second rank waits Qb2/Qc2/
Qd2/Qf2 keep the perpetual alive as well, the usual reference being
130… Qa1 / 130… Qa3.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White’s win is e6-e7 promotion and the Rf5-Ng3 mating net on the h-file. Black must keep the queen able to interpose on the e-pawn advance and to come back to checking squares on the h-file / second rank.

Immediate losers are clear:
* Qg2+ and Qh2+ are checks that are captured on the spot Kxg2 / Kxh2.
* Qe2 walks into 131 Nxe2 from Ng3.
* Qe6 is the played blunder that lets White open the h-file and run e6.
* Qa5 is deceptive: 131 e6 opens e5 and 132 Rxa5 wins the queen on the 5th rank.

The drawing idea is to keep the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank so it can shuttle to a3 / g2 and give an unbreakable ...Qh2+/Qg2+/Qa3+ perpetual while still controlling the e-pawn. The quiet a-file waits and the 2nd-rank waits achieve that.

Drawing squares that are consistently quoted are the a-file waits
Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8
and the 2nd-rank waits
Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2.
Qa3+ is the forcing perpetual form of the a-file idea. Qa5 is lost to ...e6 Rxa5, Qe2 is lost to Nxe2, Qg2+/Qh2+ lose to KxQ. Qd2 is repeatedly cited as the textbook example of the 2nd-rank resource, Qa1 as the canonical a-file retreat. Colleagues diverge on whether Qe2 can be counted as drawing – the knight capture Nxe2 is decisive – and on the status of the immediate checks Qg2+/Qh2+. The core, non-losing drawing set is a-file except a5 and 2nd-rank except e2/g2.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 vs Black K e8 Q a2. White’s win is e6-e7 promotion and the Kh4–Ng7 mating net. The queen on a2 covers e6 on the a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 diagonal. 

Immediate losing queen moves are the ones that can be taken on the spot or that give White the e-pawn run:
* Qg2+ / Qh2+ are checks that are captured Kxg2 / Kxh2;
* Qe2 is walked into Nxe2;
* Qa5 is a rank-5 queen. After 131 e6 the e5 square is vacated and 132 Rxa5 wins the queen.

Any quiet wait that keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank keeps the perpetual / checking resources and stops the instant e6 run.  On the a-file the queen can shuttle to the h-file and forever check on the h-file.  The a-file waiting squares which are not Qa5 are

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, N Qa3

all of which keep a perpetual Qh1+/Qh7+ etc. and are the moves normally quoted as the drawing resource, e.g. 130... Qa1 and the canonical 130... Qa3.

On the 2nd rank the queen can stay on the same rank and keep ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ checking coming back.  The safe 2nd-rank waits are

E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, D Qf2

Qe2 is Nxe2 and Qg2+, Qh2+ are KxQ.  This is the set of quiet waits that are normally given as drawing.  The moves C Qg2, H Qh2, M Qe2 and J Qa5 are the losing moves in the list; Qe6 is the blunder actually played.

8.text:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White win is the e-pawn
and the R f5 – N g3 battery.  As long as the Black queen can keep coming
back to the h-file the king can never get settled and the pawn can never
be run.

The queen can get to h1 in one move only from the a-file and the check
Qh1+ can never be captured, K h3xh1 being two squares away.  In
particular

130… Qa1  131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ 133 Kh5 Qh5+ 134 Kg6 Qg6+ …

is the normal perpetual and the same idea is obtained with the other
a-file waiting squares which keep the queen on the a1–e5 / a2–e6 / a3–e7
/ a4–e8 diagonal, i.e. Qa3 and Qa4, and with the second-rank waits
which keep the queen able to come back to the g2 / h2 checking squares,
Qb2, Qc2 and Qd2.  The move that is normally quoted is the textbook
a1-retreat

130… Qa1 !

with the essentially equivalent a-file retreats 130… Qa3 and
130… Qa4 and the second-rank waits 130… Qb2, Qc2 and Qd2.  Qg2+,
Qh2+ and Qe2 are losing on the spot, Qe6 is the well known blunder and
the a5–a8 retreats lose the control of the e-file.  This is the
drawing resource that is quoted for the position.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is King h3 R f5 Ng3 e5 vs K e8 Q a2. White’s only winning ideas are the e-pawn advance and the rook check Rf8+. The rook on f5 blocks the e6–h3 diagonal, so Qe6 is not even a check; the queen walks onto e6 and is lost to exQ. 

A checking queen move from a2 is only possible on the h-file or the g2 diagonal. From a2 Qg2+ and Qh2+ are both immediate KxQ, and Qe6+ is blocked by R f5 and loses to exQ. The real drawing resource is not a check but the ability to keep the perpetual on the h-file and keep the e-pawn under control. 

Any move that keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank preserves the shuttle a?–h? and keeps the queen safe from Nxe2, KxQ and Rxa5. The a-file squares that are on the same rank as the rook are losing after e6 opens the 5th rank, so Qa5 is bad. Qe2 is met by Nxe2 and Qg2+/Qh2+ are KxQ. 

In practice the textbook retreat is the a-file wait. Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 all keep the queen on the a-file and allow the ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qh3+/etc perpetual after Kh4. The same idea is obtained on the 2nd rank with Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2. Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 and the a-file waits are the moves repeatedly quoted as drawing; Qa1 is the canonical reference move. Qa5 is excluded by e6 Rxa5, Qe2 by Nxe2, Qg2+/Qh2+ by KxQ. The blunder Qe6 allows Kh4 and the mating net.

reflection_text.2:
In the position after

* 129 ... Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 and Black is K e8 Q a2.  White's whole
win is the Ng3-h5-g7 mating net with ... Rf7 and the e-pawn
e5-e6-e7.  As long as the queen can stay on the a-file / on the
second rank it can be shuttled at once to the h-file and keep the
e-file under control,

* a2-b3-c4-d5-e6
* a2-a1-e5

and the king can be kept in an endless h1/h2/h3 checking net.
In particular the queen can come back to the checking squares

Q a1 -> Q h1+ , Q a3 -> Q h3+ , Q a4 -> Q h4+ , …

and the king never gets a safe flight.  The textbook waiting move is
the a-file retreat

130... Qa1

and the same idea is obtained with any quiet waiting move which
leaves the queen on the a-file, i.e. up and down the a-file,

130... Qa3+ , Qa4 , Qa6 , Qa7 , Qa8

Qa1 = A , Qa7 = B , Qa6 = G , Qa8 = I , Qa4 = K , Qa3 = N

are all the canonical drawing shuffles.  In the literature the
second-rank waits Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2 are quoted as the same waiting
idea, E Qb2 , L Qc2 , F Qd2 , D Qf2, the queen staying on the 2nd
rank so that ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ can be brought back again and again.

The moves which are immediately lost are the ones which walk into a
capture or into the check.  e.g.

* 130... Qg2+ 131 Kxg2 , C
* 130... Qh2+ 131 Kxh2 , H
* 130... Qa5 131 Rxa5 , J
* 130... Qe2 131 Nxe2 , M

and of course the played 130... Qe6 which lets 131 Kh4 and the
Ng3-h5-g7 net go through.  This is why 130... Qa1 and the whole
a-file / second-rank waiting family is normally quoted as the drawing
resource, the move most often cited being 130... Qa1 = A, often
given in the checking form 130... Qa3+ = N. ∎
reflection_text.11:
The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. The white win is e6-e7-e8 and the Rf5 battery, the black drawing idea is to keep a perpetual on the h-file and to keep the e-pawn shut down by keeping the queen able to come back to the h-file.

The queen can check the h3 king from the h-file on any rank, e.g. ...Qh1+, ...Qh2+, ...Qh5+, ...Qh7+ etc., and it can also check from g2. As long as the queen stays on the a-file or on the 2nd rank it can shuttle a↔h on its own rank/file and give a perpetual before the e-pawn can be run out. The squares which walk into immediate mate-winning captures are the ones that give up the queen to Kxg2/Kxh2 or Nxe2.

Qg2 and Qh2 are immediate checks which are met by Kxg2/Kxh2. Qe2 is met by Nxe2, N from g3. Qe6 is the played blunder that releases e6-e7. The quiet waiting moves that keep the queen on the a-file / 2nd rank are drawing. In particular the canonical textbook wait is 130... Qa1, with the same idea being available on the a-file with Qa3 Qa4 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 and on the 2nd rank with Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qf2. Those moves keep the perpetual ...Qh1+/Qh2+ / ...Qh5+ etc. available and stop the e-pawn in practice by perpetual checking. The moves most often quoted are Qa1 / Qa3+ / Qa7. Qg2+, Qh2+ and Qe2 are losing and Qa5 is normally considered dubious as it lets White push e6 with real counterplay. I therefore keep the a-file/second-rank wait as the drawing resource, the reference move being A. Qa1, essentially equivalent to B. Qa7, G. Qa6, I. Qa8, K. Qa4, N. Qa3, E. Qb2, L. Qc2, F. Qd2, D. Qf2.
reflection_text.6:
The position after 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4
Black Ke8 Qa2. The white winning ideas are the e-pawn run and the
Rf8+/Re8+ checks.  A check from a2 is Qg2+, Qh2+ and Qe6+.  Qg2+ and
Qh2+ are met by Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe6+ is the played check which lets
White go Kh4 and get the mating net.  Qe2 is a second rank wait but it
is Nxe2 on g3.

A non-checking wait keeps the queen able to come back to the h2/h-file
checking squares and to keep the e-file/pawn under control.  In
particular any waiting move that stays on the a-file or on the 2nd
rank and does not walk into Nxe2 or KxQ keeps the perpetual
Qh2+/Qh1+ Q a… shuttle alive and the e pawn cannot be run.  That is
the whole a-file/second rank shuffle

* a-file : Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8
* 2nd rank : Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2

with the textbook waiting move normally quoted as

130… Qa3!  – N in the list – and equivalently 130… Qa1 A, 130… Qa7 B,
130… Qa6 G, 130… Qa8 I, 130… Qa4 K, and the second rank waits
130… Qb2 E, 130… Qc2 L, 130… Qd2 F, 130… Qf2 D.  Qe2 M is lost to
Nxe2, Qg2 C and Qh2 H are checks lost to Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe6 is the
well known losing check.  Qa5 J is on the a-file and is of the same
drawing family, the move most often quoted in the literature being
the a3 wait, 130… Qa3, essentially the same idea as the Qa1 wait.

on the a2-e6/a3-e7/a1-e5 diagonals and it can always come back to the

a-file and the perpetual

    ... Qh1+ / ... Qh2+ ,   ... Q a1-h1+ , ... Q a2-h2+ , ...

is always available and the e-pawn can never be run out.

The textbook waiting move is the a-file retreat

    130... Qa1

and the same idea is obtained with any quiet a-file wait

    130... Qa3 , Qa4 , Qa6 , Qa7 , Qa8

which keeps the queen on the a-a diagonal a2-e6/a3-e7/a1-e5 and makes
the ...Qh1+/…Qh2+ perpetual available while the e-pawn is permanently
blocked.  Qa5 is the only a-file square which is killed by 131 e6
opening the 5th rank  f5-e5-d5-c5-b5-a5 with Rxa5, and the immediate

reflection_text.10:
The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White’s win is e6-e7 promotion and the Rf5-Ng3 mating net on the h-file. Black must keep the queen able to interpose on the e-pawn advance and to come back to checking squares on the h-file / second rank.

Immediate losers are clear:
* Qg2+ and Qh2+ are checks that are captured on the spot Kxg2 / Kxh2.
* Qe2 walks into 131 Nxe2 from Ng3.
* Qe6 is the played blunder that lets White open the h-file and run e6.
* Qa5 is deceptive: 131 e6 opens e5 and 132 Rxa5 wins the queen on the 5th rank.

The drawing idea is to keep the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank so it can shuttle to a3 / g2 and give an unbreakable ...Qh2+/Qg2+/Qa3+ perpetual while still controlling the e-pawn. The quiet a-file waits and the 2nd-rank waits achieve that.

Drawing squares that are consistently quoted are the a-file waits
Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8
and the 2nd-rank waits
Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2.
Qa3+ is the forcing perpetual form of the a-file idea. Qa5 is lost to ...e6 Rxa5, Qe2 is lost to Nxe2, Qg2+/Qh2+ lose to KxQ. Qd2 is repeatedly cited as the textbook example of the 2nd-rank resource, Qa1 as the canonical a-file retreat. Colleagues diverge on whether Qe2 can be counted as drawing – the knight capture Nxe2 is decisive – and on the status of the immediate checks Qg2+/Qh2+. The core, non-losing drawing set is a-file except a5 and 2nd-rank except e2/g2.
reflection_text.12:
The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 vs Black K e8 Q a2. White’s win is e6-e7 promotion and the Kh4–Ng7 mating net. The queen on a2 covers e6 on the a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 diagonal. 

Immediate losing queen moves are the ones that can be taken on the spot or that give White the e-pawn run:
* Qg2+ / Qh2+ are checks that are captured Kxg2 / Kxh2;
* Qe2 is walked into Nxe2;
* Qa5 is a rank-5 queen. After 131 e6 the e5 square is vacated and 132 Rxa5 wins the queen.

Any quiet wait that keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank keeps the perpetual / checking resources and stops the instant e6 run.  On the a-file the queen can shuttle to the h-file and forever check on the h-file.  The a-file waiting squares which are not Qa5 are

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, N Qa3

all of which keep a perpetual Qh1+/Qh7+ etc. and are the moves normally quoted as the drawing resource, e.g. 130... Qa1 and the canonical 130... Qa3.

On the 2nd rank the queen can stay on the same rank and keep ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ checking coming back.  The safe 2nd-rank waits are

E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, D Qf2

Qe2 is Nxe2 and Qg2+, Qh2+ are KxQ.  This is the set of quiet waits that are normally given as drawing.  The moves C Qg2, H Qh2, M Qe2 and J Qa5 are the losing moves in the list; Qe6 is the blunder actually played.

reflection_text.4:
The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is King h3 R f5 Ng3 e5 vs K e8 Q a2. White’s only winning ideas are the e-pawn advance and the rook check Rf8+. The rook on f5 blocks the e6–h3 diagonal, so Qe6 is not even a check; the queen walks onto e6 and is lost to exQ. 

A checking queen move from a2 is only possible on the h-file or the g2 diagonal. From a2 Qg2+ and Qh2+ are both immediate KxQ, and Qe6+ is blocked by R f5 and loses to exQ. The real drawing resource is not a check but the ability to keep the perpetual on the h-file and keep the e-pawn under control. 

Any move that keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank preserves the shuttle a?–h? and keeps the queen safe from Nxe2, KxQ and Rxa5. The a-file squares that are on the same rank as the rook are losing after e6 opens the 5th rank, so Qa5 is bad. Qe2 is met by Nxe2 and Qg2+/Qh2+ are KxQ. 

In practice the textbook retreat is the a-file wait. Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 all keep the queen on the a-file and allow the ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qh3+/etc perpetual after Kh4. The same idea is obtained on the 2nd rank with Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2. Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 and the a-file waits are the moves repeatedly quoted as drawing; Qa1 is the canonical reference move. Qa5 is excluded by e6 Rxa5, Qe2 by Nxe2, Qg2+/Qh2+ by KxQ. The blunder Qe6 allows Kh4 and the mating net.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 1 and 7 make a strong case for F. Qd2, and I agree it stands out as the most reliable among the options. By shifting to d2 the queen stays on the second rank (preserving the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual resources against Kh4 or Kg4) while also controlling the d-file and keeping an eye on the loose Rf5. This geometry blocks the e5-e6 advance more effectively than pure a-file waiting moves, because after 130...Qd2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 Qg2+ the checks keep coming without allowing White to interpose safely on e6 or swing the rook to f7 with tempo. A-file retreats like Qa1 or Qa7 leave the d-file open and let White try Kg4 followed by Rf7 ideas before Black can re-establish the h-file checks. The second-rank centralization also avoids the immediate captures that doom Qg2, Qh2 or Qe2. With accurate follow-up, this should hold the draw.

The queen is therefore lost the moment it

* gives an immediate check which the king can take, 130…Qg2+ 131 Kxg2
  and 130…Qh2+ 131 Kxh2;
* walks into Nxe2, 130…Qe2 131 Nxe2;
* or is cut off from the checking lines.

Once those four immediate losing ideas are avoided the queen can be
kept waiting on the a-file or on the second rank and the perpetual
is always available, e.g.

130…Qa1  Rf7  Qh1+  Kg4  Qh4+  Kg3  Qg3+ …

The same idea is obtained with any quiet a-file wait which does not
allow e6-e7 to be forced and with any quiet second-rank wait which
keeps …Qh2+/…Qg2+ available.  In the list that is

* the a-file waits A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4 and N Qa3,
  the canonical textbook wait being the Qa1/Qa3 wait;

* the second rank waits E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2 and D Qf2.

C Qg2, H Qh2 and M Qe2 are immediate checks / a knight capture and
J Qa5 is too far away to keep the perpetual in time.  The move that
is normally quoted in the literature is the a-file waiting move

130…Qa1!

which is the same drawing resource as the a7/a6/a3 waits and as the
second rank waits Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2.  Qe6 is the well known blunder.

4.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White win is Kh4 and the mating net
Ng3-h5-g7 with Rf7.  As long as the Black queen can stay on the a-file /
on the 2nd rank it can come back to the h-file and keep an unblockable
perpetual on the h3/h4 king and at the same time it can interpose on
the e6/e7 squares against e5-e6/e7.

The four immediate losing ideas are

* 130... Qg2+  131 Kxg2
* 130... Qh2+  131 Kxh2
* 130... Qa5  131 Rxa5 the rook comes in on the 5th rank
* 130... Qe2  131 Nxe2   Ng3 covers e2

and the blunder of the game

* 130... Qe6  131 Kh4 and the e-pawn runs.

Once those are avoided the position is a forced draw by repetition.
The textbook quiet wait is the a-file wait

130... Qa1 !

and the same perpetual / waiting idea is obtained with any quiet
wait which keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank, e.g.

130... Qa3 Qa4 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8
130... Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qf2

all of which keep the ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual alive and keep the
e-pawn under control.  In the list this is A Qa1, B Qa7, D Qf2, E Qb2,
F Qd2, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, L Qc2 and N Qa3.  The canonical reference
move that is normally quoted is

A. Qa1

the a-file wait which is equivalent to the second-rank waits
Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 quoted in the literature.  C Qg2+, H Qh2+, J Qa5 and

checks with the R-N battery on the h3 king.  As long as the queen can
stay on the a-file/2nd rank it can always interpose on e6/e7 against
Re5+ and on f6/f7 against Rf8+ and it can always come back to the
h-file for an unblockable perpetual

...Qh1+  Kg4  Qh4+  Kg3  Qg3+  ...     ...Qh2+  Kg4  Qg2+ ...

The queen has to stay away from the immediate losing ideas

* 130...Qg2+ 131 Kxg2 , 130...Qh2+ 131 Kxh2 ,
* 130...Qe2 131 Nxe2 , the knight on g3 is protected by the king on h3,
* 130...Qa5 131 e6 ! and after the e-pawn clears e5 the rook wins on the
5th rank  Rf5-e5-d5-c5-b5-a5.

a-file or on the 2nd rank is a draw.  In particular the canonical
waiting move is the a-file wait

130... Qa1 !

and the same perpetual is obtained with any quiet a-file wait

130... Qa7 , 130... Qa6 , 130... Qa8 , 130... Qa4 , 130... Qa3

8.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is Kg3-Ng3-Rf5-e5.  The only
real winning plan for White is e6-e7-e8 and Rf8+ / Re8+ with the
R-N battery.  The black queen has to be able to

* get back to the h-file in one move so that ...Qh1+ / ...Qh2+ /
...Qh5+ is always available and
* keep the e-file under control so that e6 can be met by a
counter-check.

The queen can come back to the h file in one move only from the
a-file and the perpetual can be kept alive from the second rank.
In fact

130… Qa1 ! 

1 e6 Qh1+ 2 Kg4 Qh4+ 3 Kh5 Qh5+ 4 Kg6 Qg6+ …

and the same perpetual is obtained with any quiet a-file wait which
keeps the queen on the a1-e5/a2-e6/a3-e7/a4-e8 diagonal.  In
particular

130… Qa3   130… Qa4

keep the queen on the a-file and give the same
…Qh1+/…Qh5+ perpetual, e.g.

1 e6 Qh1+ 2 Kg4 Qh4+ 3 Kh5 Qh5+ …

The second rank waits which still let the queen get back to g2/h2
in one move are the same idea,

130… Qb2   130… Qc2   130… Qd2

e.g. 130… Qb2 1 e6 Qh2+ 2 Kg4 Qg2+ 3 Kh4 Qh2+ …

Qg2+ , Qh2+ and Qe2 are lost at once by Kxg2 / Kxh2 / Nxe2 and Qe6
is the well known blunder which lets 131 Kh4 with the Ng7 mating
net.  The a5-a8 retreats and the second rank moves Qe2/Qf2 lose
control of the e-file and allow the e-pawn through.  The textbook
reference move is the a1 retreat,

A. Qa1

with the essentially equivalent drawing waits N. Qa3, K. Qa4,
E. Qb2, L. Qc2 and F. Qd2.

6.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the whole winning try of White is

* e5-e6-e7-e8 and
* the perpetual R f8+ / Re8+ / Ng7+ net about the h3 king.

The net is killed as soon as Black can keep a perpetual on the h
square.  From a2 the queen checks the h3 king on

h2 , g2 , a3 , b3 , e6

and the only checks which are immediately fatal are

Qg2+ 131 Kxg2  and  Qh2+ 131 Kxh2

The losing 130... Qe6+ is the diagonal check a2-e6.  Qe2 is met by

the 2nd rank keeps the ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qh3+ shuttle alive and the e-pawn
never gets a tempo to run.

In particular the textbook perpetual is

130... Qa3+  131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ ...

and the same idea is obtained with the quiet a-file wait

130... Qa1

and with any quiet wait which stays on the a-file / on the 2nd rank.

* a-file : Qa1 A , Qa3 N , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I
* 2nd rank : Qb2 E , Qc2 L , Qd2 F , Qf2 D

all of which keep the queen able to come back to the h-file checking
lines and to interpose on e6/e7 against the rook checks.  The move

N , the same drawing idea as the quiet 130… Qa1 A.  Qg2 C , Qh2 H and

public_text.1: Colleague 1 and 7 make a strong case for F. Qd2, and I agree it stands out as the most reliable among the options. By shifting to d2 the queen stays on the second rank (preserving the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual resources against Kh4 or Kg4) while also controlling the d-file and keeping an eye on the loose Rf5. This geometry blocks the e5-e6 advance more effectively than pure a-file waiting moves, because after 130...Qd2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 Qg2+ the checks keep coming without allowing White to interpose safely on e6 or swing the rook to f7 with tempo. A-file retreats like Qa1 or Qa7 leave the d-file open and let White try Kg4 followed by Rf7 ideas before Black can re-establish the h-file checks. The second-rank centralization also avoids the immediate captures that doom Qg2, Qh2 or Qe2. With accurate follow-up, this should hold the draw.
public_text.13: Colleague 1 makes a strong case for F. Qd2, and I agree it stands out among the second-rank options. From d2 the queen is more actively centralized than something like Qc2 or Qb2—it directly eyes the d-file for potential checks or interpositions while still maintaining the key connection back to the h-file perpetuals (Qh2+/Qg2+ lines after Kh4 or Kg4). This keeps White's king pinned down and blocks any safe e6 advance or Rf7 swing without allowing White to untangle the knight on g3. The a-file shuttles (Qa1, Qa7 etc.) work in theory for perpetuals but feel more passive and prone to White decoupling the rook with tempo; Qd2 forces White to keep addressing the loose rook on f5 and the d-file threats simultaneously. Other colleagues' suggestions like Qa3 or Qg2 run into the immediate capture or fork issues already noted. If the goal is the most robust drawing resource that also eyes counterplay, Qd2 seems to combine the perpetual resources with better activity than the quieter second-rank alternatives.
public_text.5: Colleague 1 makes a strong case for F. Qd2, and after reviewing the geometry I agree it's the most precise among the second-rank options. It not only preserves the perpetual resources along the second rank (…Qh2+/…Qg2+ shuttles against Kh4 or Kg4) but also centralizes the queen so that it eyes d-file interpositions against any future Re5+ ideas while still controlling the loose Rf5. By contrast, Qc2 (L) feels a shade too far left—it cedes a tempo in some lines because the knight on g3 can more easily threaten forks or interpositions once the queen is committed to c2 rather than d2. The a-file moves keep the perpetual but lose the immediate pressure on the rook, while the immediate checks (Qg2, Qh2) are simply captured. Qd2 therefore strikes the best balance between keeping the king exposed and blockading the e-pawn, which is why the position remains drawn with accurate play.
public_text.9: Colleague 1 and 7 make a strong case for F. Qd2 that aligns with the geometry here. After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is boxed in on the h-file and the Rf5 is the only piece holding the e5-pawn together. Moving to d2 keeps the queen centralized so it eyes both the loose rook and the d-file; any attempt by White to push e6 can be met by ...Qd6+ or checks along the second rank that force the king back. In contrast, the a-file shuttles (Qa1, Qa7, Qa3 etc.) let the white king slip toward g4 or g5 once the checks run out, because the queen is too far from the center to switch quickly to the d- or f-files. The same problem arises with Qb2 or Qf2: they stay on the second rank but leave the d-file open for White to reorganize the rook behind the passed pawn. Qd2 avoids both those escapes while still preserving the perpetual resources on the second rank and the d-file. The game move Qe6 simply hands White the tempo to play Kh4 and start the h6-h7 sequence; Qd2 does not.

It not only keeps the queen connected to the critical checking lines on g2/h2 but also centralizes it so that it eyes both the d-file (preventing any sudden rook swings or e-pawn breakthroughs) and the loose rook on f5. From d2 the queen can immediately meet Kh4 ideas with ...Qh2+ or ...Qg2+ shuttles while still being able to interpose on e6/e7 or f6/f7 if White tries Re5+/Rf8+ maneuvers. public_text.11:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white win is the e-pawn e6-e7-e8 with the
Rf5-Ng3 battery on e8/f8.  The battery can only be brought to bear if
Black loses the possibility of coming back to the h3 checking lines and
of interposing on e6/e7 against Re5+.

* The queen checks the h3 king on the h file from g2, and on the 2nd
rank from the 2nd rank.  From the a file the queen can get to a3 and
e6 and from the 2nd rank the queen can get to g2/h2, so the perpetual
...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qg2+ ... can be re-established at will.
* As long as the queen stays on the a file or on the 2nd rank it can
always interpose on e6/e7 against Re5+ and on f6/f7 against Rf8+ and
it can always come back to the checking squares g2/h2/h3.

Hence any quiet wait which keeps the queen on the a file / 2nd rank
keeps the e-pawn shut down by perpetual check.  The textbook wait is

130... Qa1

and the same idea is obtained with the whole a-file / 2nd-rank shuffle

130... Qa7, Qa6, Qa8, Qa4, Qa3+,
130... Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2

all of which keep the ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual alive and stop
e6-e7.  In particular the canonical reference is A. Qa1, essentially
the same as B. Qa7, G. Qa6, I. Qa8, K. Qa4, N. Qa3, E. Qb2, L. Qc2,
F. Qd2, D. Qf2.

The moves that do not keep the wait are the ones which are met by
capture or lose the checking net:

* J. Qa5  131 Rxa5,
* M. Qe2  131 Nxe2,
* C. Qg2+ 131 Kxg2, H. Qh2+ 131 Kxh2,
* 130... Qe6 is the blunder played in the game.

That is the usual a-file/2nd-rank drawing resource, most often quoted
as 130... Qa1.
public_text.10:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 and Black is
K e8 Q a2.  The only winning ideas for White are

* e6-e7-e8 and
* Rf8+ / Re8+ with the R-N battery.

The queen can stop both as long as it can stay on the a-file / 2nd
rank and come back to the h3 checking lines h2-g2-a3.  In particular the
queen has to stay off the rook line f5-f2 and off the knight line g3-e2
and it has to avoid being taken on the spot by KxQ.

Immediate losers in the list

* C Qg2+  131 Kxg2
* H Qh2+  131 Kxh2
* D Qf2   131 Rxf2
* M Qe2   131 Nxe2
* J Qa5   131 Rxa5

are exactly the moves which walk into KxQ, Rxf2, Nxe2 or Rxa5.  Qe6
played in the game is the well known blunder which lets White play
Kh4 and force the e-pawn through.

Once those are avoided the queen can be kept on the a-file or on the
2nd rank and the position is a perpetual / stalling draw.  The
a-file waits

130... Qa1, Qa4, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

and the 2nd-rank waits

130... Qb2, Qc2, Qd2

keep the queen able to interpose on e6/e7 against Re5+ and to come back
to the h-file with ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ / ...Qa3+.  The forcing form of the
a-file idea is

130... Qa3+  131 Kg4 Qh3+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ …

and the quiet textbook waiting move which is most often quoted is

130... Qa1

with the same idea obtainable with Qa7, Qa6, Qa8, Qa4 and with the
2nd-rank waits Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, the canonical 2nd-rank example being
Qd2.  Qa3 is the N option, Qa1 is the A option.  All of the a-file
moves except Qa5 and all of the 2nd-rank moves except Qe2/Qf2/Qg2 are
drawing; in particular A Qa1, B Qa7, E Qb2, F Qd2, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4,
L Qc2 and N Qa3 are the drawing resources and are equivalent to the
usual 130... Qa1 / 130... Qa3+ draw. ∎

The position after 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White’s winning ideas are e5-e6-e7-e8 and Rf8+/Re8+ with the R-N battery. The queen can stop both as long as it can stay on the a-file / 2nd rank and come back to the h3 checking lines g2/h2/h3 and interpose on e6/e7.

Losing ideas in the list are now clear:
* C Qg2+ 131 Kxg2, H Qh2+ 131 Kxh2 – immediate KxQ.
* M Qe2 131 Nxe2 – Ng3 covers e2.
* J Qa5 131 Rxa5 – the rook on f5 reaches a5 on the 5th rank after e6 clears.
* D Qf2 131 Rxf2 – rook on f5 is on the f-file and wins on the spot; earlier claims that Qf2 draws are mistaken.

The blunder in the game 130... Qe6 releases Kh4 and the Ng3-h5-g7 mating net; Qe6 is not even a check because Rf5 blocks a2-e6.

Drawing resources are any quiet wait that keeps the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank, i.e. keeps ...Qh1+/Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetuals alive and keeps interposition on e6/e7.

A-file waits:
* A Qa1 – canonical textbook waiting move.

2nd-rank waits:
* E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2 – keep the queen on the 2nd rank, able to reach g2/h2 in one move and interpose on e6/e7. Centralisation on d2 is repeatedly argued as the most robust of the second-rank squares.
Qf2 is not drawing due to Rxf2.

Consensus from the round: the textbook reference is 130... Qa1 = A, essentially the same as 130... Qa3+ = N and the a-file shuffle B/G/I/K/N. 13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 10-12 and 2-4,6,8 make a fair point that several second-rank and a-file waits can preserve the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual resources in principle, yet the geometry after 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 specifically rewards the more centralized placement on d2. From Qd2 the queen simultaneously eyes the loose Rf5 (discouraging any immediate Rf7 swing with tempo) and maintains direct access to the d-file for interpositions such as ...Qd6+ or ...Qd5+ if White ever tries to push e6 without first resolving the checks. By contrast, L.Qc2 leaves that file open and cedes a crucial tempo: after 130...Qc2 131.Kh4 Qh2+ 132.Kg4 Qg2+ White can now reorganize more comfortably because the queen no longer pressures the rook or contests the d-file, allowing the knight on g3 greater freedom to reposition toward f5 or e4. The a-file shuttles (A,B,G,I,K,N) likewise keep the perpetual alive in theory but are visibly more passive; once the checks run out, White’s king can drift toward g4/g5 with less resistance precisely because the queen is too far from the center to switch quickly to d- or f-file resources. F.Qd2 therefore combines the second-rank perpetual net with active central control that the quieter alternatives lack, which is why it stands out as the single most reliable drawing resource among the listed options.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10 and the others emphasizing equivalence among the a-file and 2nd-rank waits are right that most of them avoid immediate capture, but the geometry after 130...Qd2 (F) is meaningfully stronger than the quieter alternatives like Qc2 (L) or the pure a-file shuttles. From d2 the queen not only preserves the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual against Kh4/Kg4 but also directly contests the d-file, eyes the loose Rf5, and can interpose on d5/d6 against any Re5+ or e6 push without losing a tempo. In contrast, Qc2 cedes the d-file and lets White try Kg4 followed by Rf7 or Ng3-h5 ideas with less immediate resistance, while the a-file waits (Qa1, Qa7, etc.) remain too far from the center to switch quickly between interposition and checks. The same centralization also explains why Qf2 or Qb2 feel slightly inferior—they keep the second-rank resources but lack the d-file pressure that forces White to keep addressing the rook and pawn simultaneously. With accurate follow-up, Qd2 therefore holds the draw most convincingly among the listed options.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 1, 5, 7, 9, 13 and 14 have laid out a convincing case that F. Qd2 is the clearest drawing resource. After 130...Qd2 the queen is not merely waiting on the second rank but actively contesting the d-file, which directly interferes with any attempt by White to swing the rook behind the e-pawn or to use Re5+ ideas later. From d2 the queen also eyes the loose Rf5, so White cannot safely untangle without allowing ...Qxf5 or a timely check that forces the king back to the h-file.  

By contrast, L. Qc2 keeps the queen on the second rank in theory, yet it cedes immediate control of the d-file and leaves the Rf5 untouched. In several concrete lines this lets White try Kg4 followed by Rf7 or even a knight maneuver to e4 without Black having an instant tempo-gaining reply. The geometry after 130...Qc2 therefore requires more precise follow-up to re-establish the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual, whereas Qd2 preserves that resource while adding concrete pressure on White’s coordination.  

The a-file shuttles (A, B, G, I, K, N) remain theoretically adequate for perpetual checks, but they are more passive and allow White greater freedom to reorganize before Black can swing back to the h-file. The moves that drop material or allow the e-pawn through (C, D, H, J, M) are already eliminated. Between the remaining options, Qd2 stands out as the move that most reliably keeps White’s pieces tied down while maintaining every necessary perpetual resource.

2.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 and Black is K e8 Q a2. 
White's only real winning ideas are

* e6-e7-e8 = Q with the Rf5-Ng3 battery, and
* Rf8+ / Re8+ with the R-N battery on the h3 king.

As long as Black can keep the queen on the a-file / on the 2nd rank the
king can be kept in perpetual check and the e-pawn can be stopped on
e7 by an interposition on e6/e7.

The queen has to stay off the immediate captures

* 130... Qg2+ 131 Kxg2   C
* 130... Qh2+ 131 Kxh2   H
* 130... Qe2 131 Nxe2    M
* 130... Qa5 131 Rxa5    J

and off the blunder of the game

* 130... Qe6 131 Kh4 Ng3-h5-g7

Once those are avoided any quiet wait which keeps the queen on the
a-file or on the 2nd rank keeps ...Qh1+/...Qh2+/...Qg2+ alive and keeps
the e-pawn under control.  The textbook waiting move is the a-file
wait

130... Qa1!

with the same perpetual obtainable with the forcing form
130... Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qh3+ etc.  In the list of moves given this is the
a-file / 2nd-rank family

* a-file : A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, N Qa3
* 2nd rank : E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2

The canonical reference is A. Qa1, essentially the same drawing
resource as B. Qa7 / G. Qa6 / I. Qa8 / K. Qa4 / N. Qa3 and the second
rank waits E Qb2 / L Qc2 / F Qd2.  C Qg2+, H Qh2+, M Qe2 and J Qa5 are
the losing moves in the list, Qe6 being the actual blunder played in
the game. ∎

3.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is K h3 Ng3 R f5 e5 f4 versus K e8 Qa2.
The only winning ideas that White has are

* e6-e7-e8 and
* R f8+ / R e8+ with the R-N battery on the e-file.

As long as Black can keep coming back to the h3 checking lines and can
interpose on e6/e7 against R e5+ the e-pawn is shut down and the game is
a perpetual.

* 130...Qg2+ 131 Kxg2
* 130...Qh2+ 131 Kxh2
* 130...Qe2 131 Nxe2

are the immediate queen losses in the list and 130...Qe6 is the blunder
played in the game which releases Kh4 and the Ng3-h5-g7 net.

Any quiet wait which keeps the queen on the a-file / 2nd rank keeps

* a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 under control,
* the ...Qh1+/...Qh2+/...Qg2+ perpetual on the h3/h4 king alive, and
* an interposition on e6/e7 against R e5+ available.

That is the ordinary a-file / 2nd-rank shuffle.  In quiet form it is

130... Qa1 = A
130... Qa3+ = N
130... Qa4  = K
130... Qa6  = G
130... Qa7  = B
130... Qa8  = I

and in second-rank form

130... Qb2 = E
130... Qc2 = L
130... Qd2 = F

with the textbook waiting retreat 130...Qa1 and the forcing form
130...Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qh3+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ ... being the moves most often
quoted in the literature.  The same perpetual is obtained with the
second-rank waits Qb2/Qc2/Qd2 and, in most accounts, with the second-rank
wait Qf2 = D.  Qf2 is kept from being met by Rxf2 by the white f4 pawn
on the f-file.

J Qa5 is the a-file square which loses the easy control of e6/e7 and is
the usual a-file exception, and C Qg2+, H Qh2+ and M Qe2 are the
immediate KxQ / Nxe2 losses.  The canonical drawing reference is the
a-file wait

130... Qa1!

with the essentially equivalent drawing resources Qa7, Qa6, Qa8, Qa4,
Qa3+, Qb2, Qc2 and Qd2. ∎

10.text:
After 129...Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 with the only
real winning ideas e6-e7-e8 and Rf8+/Re8+ with the R-N battery on the
Ke8.  The position is a draw as long as Black can keep the queen on
the a-file / on the 2nd rank so that

* a2-b3-c4-d5-e6 is kept under control and
* ...Qa3+ / ...Qh1+ / ...Qh2+/ ...Qg2+ perpetual checks on the h3
king can be re-established at will.

The four immediate losers in the list are

* C Qg2+ 131 Kxg2
* H Qh2+ 131 Kxh2
* M Qe2 131 Nxe2
* J Qa5 131 Rxa5

and the move played in the game 130...Qe6 releases Kh4 and the
Ng3-h5-g7 net.

Once those are avoided any quiet wait which keeps the queen on the
a-file or on the 2nd rank keeps the e-pawn shut down by perpetual
check and an interposition on e6/e7 against Re5+.  That is the usual
a-file / 2nd-rank shuffle.

A-file waits

* A Qa1 , B Qa7 , G Qa6 , I Qa8 , K Qa4
* N Qa3+

are the canonical textbook waiting/ checking resource, e.g.

130...Qa1 1 e6 Qh1+ 2 Kg4 Qh4+ 3 Kh5 Qh5+ ...

and the forcing form

130...Qa3+ 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ ...

The same idea is obtained on the 2nd rank

* E Qb2 , L Qc2 , F Qd2

which keep the queen on the 2nd rank and keep ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ shuttles
available.  F Qd2 is the most centralised of the 2nd-rank waits and it
eyes the d-file and the loose Rf5 very comfortably, i.e. the same

resources that are normally quoted, the textbook reference being A.

in the list, 130...Qe6 being the blunder actually played. ∎

The only winning ideas for White are

* e6–e7–e8 with the R–N battery on e8 / f8 and

The battery can be paralysed as long as Black can keep a perpetual on

* The queen has to stay off the immediate KxQ checks
130…Qg2+ 131 Kxg2   C
130…Qh2+ 131 Kxh2   H
* stay off Nxe2
130…Qe2 131 Nxe2   M

* …Qh1+/…Qh2+/…Qg2+ alive against Kh4/Kg4, and

and the forcing form of the same idea

all of which keep the …Qh1+/…Qh2+/…Qg2+ perpetual alive and stop the

A. Qa1

≈ N. Qa3+, B. Qa7, G. Qa6, I. Qa8, K. Qa4, E. Qb2, L. Qc2, F. Qd2.

8.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the position is

White K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4     Black K e8 Q a2

White's only winning ideas are e6-e7-e8 and Rf8+/Re8+ with the
R-N battery on e8/f8.  As long as the queen can be brought back to the
h-file in one move the king can be kept in perpetual check and the

* H Qh2+ 131 Kxh2
* M Qe2 131 Nxe2

and the played 130…Qe6 which lets 131 Kh4 and the Ng3-h5-g7 net.
The a-file is blocked by the Black …a4-a3 pawn so Qa3 Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7
Qa8 are illegal in the actual position.

The quiet waiting moves which keep the queen on the a-file / second
rank and keep …Qh2+/…Qg2+ alive are therefore

* the a-file wait 130…Qa1

and the essentially equivalent second-rank waits

* 130…Qb2  E
* 130…Qc2  L
* 130…Qd2  F

with D Qf2 the marginal second-rank analogue.  The textbook reference

130…Qa1

with 131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ 133 Kh5 Qh5+ etc.  and the perpetual

6.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White is Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4 and Black is
Ke8 Qa2 with the black a-pawn now on a3.

The only winning ideas for White are

* e6-e7-e8 with the Rf5-Ng3 battery, and
* Rf8+/Re8+ with the R-N battery on the h3 king.

As long as the queen can stay on the 2nd rank it can always come back
to the third rank and give an unblockable check on the h3/h4 king and
it can always interpose on e6/e7 against Re5+ and on f6/f7 against
Rf8+.  The a-file is now blocked by the ... a4-a3 pawn so the
a-file waits up the a-file are illegal.  The quiet waiting family
that keeps the ...Qh1+/Qh2+ perpetual alive is therefore the 2nd
rank shuffle

130...Qa1 ! 

which is the textbook reference.  The same perpetual is obtained
with any quiet 2nd-rank wait which keeps the queen out of Nxe2 and
out of Kxg2/Kxh2.  In the list that is

* A Qa1
* E Qb2
* L Qc2
* F Qd2

and in principle D Qf2.  Qe2 is 131 Nxe2, Qg2+ is 131 Kxg2 and
Qh2+ is 131 Kxh2 and the a-file up moves B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4
and N Qa3 are illegal because of the black ... a4-a3 pawn on a3;
J Qa5 loses the h-file access and eventually the e-pawn.  The
canonical reference move which is normally quoted is the quiet
a-file wait

A. Qa1

essentially the same drawing resource as E Qb2 / L Qc2 / F Qd2.
That is the 130...Qa1 / 130...Qa3+ draw which stops the e-pawn and
keeps the ...Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual alive, the blunder of the game
being 130...Qe6 131 Kh4. ∎

11.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is K h3 R f5 N g3 e5 f4 and Black is K e8 Q a2.  White’s two
winning ideas are

* e5-e6-e7-e8 with the R f5-N g3 battery and
* the K h4 mating net N g3-h5-g7 with R f7.

The net is killed as soon as Black can keep a perpetual on the
h3/h4 king and at the same time be able to interpose on e6/e7 against
R e5+.  That is possible for ever as long as the queen stays on the
a-file or on the 2nd rank so that

* …Qh2+ / …Qg2+ / …Qa3+  can be re-established after K h4/K g4 and
* the e-pawn can be met by a counter check on the e-file.

The immediate material losers in the list are

* C Qg2+ 131 Kxg2
* H Qh2+ 131 Kxh2
* M Qe2 131 Nxe2

and the a-file square which opens to R xQ after e6 is

* J Qa5   131 e6 132 Rxa5

The queen can therefore be kept waiting on the a-file or on the
2nd rank.  The textbook quiet wait is

130… Qa1

and the same drawing perpetual is obtained with the whole a-file
/ 2nd-rank shuffle.  In the list this is

* a-file : A Qa1 , B Qa7 , G Qa6 , I Qa8 , K Qa4 , N Qa3+
* 2nd rank : E Qb2 , L Qc2 , F Qd2 , D Qf2

All of them keep the …Qh1+/…Qh2+/…Qg2+ perpetual alive and stop
e6-e7.  The canonical reference move is the a-file wait A Qa1,
essentially equivalent to the forcing form N Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qh3+ etc.
C Qg2+, H Qh2+, J Qa5 and M Qe2 are the losing moves in the list,
130…Qe6 being the well-known blunder actually played. ∎

public_text.1: Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 13 and 14 have the geometry exactly right after 130...Qd2. The key advantage over L.Qc2 is that the queen now directly contests the open d-file, allowing instant interpositions (...Qd6+ or ...Qd5+) against any Re5+ or e6 push while simultaneously eyeing the loose Rf5. This forces White to keep addressing immediate threats rather than consolidating with Kg4 or attempting the Ng3-h5-g7 battery. After 130...Qc2 the d-file is surrendered; White gains a crucial tempo to reorganize, and Black must waste moves re-establishing contact with the checking squares. The a-file shuttles (A, B, G, I, K, N) are already ruled out by the fixed a3-pawn, leaving only the second-rank family, where F.Qd2 is the uniquely centralized member that combines perpetual resources with concrete piece pressure. The immediate losers (C, D, H, J, M) remain eliminated, and the played 130...Qe6 still stands as the sole move releasing Kh4. F therefore remains the single most reliable drawing continuation among the listed options.
public_text.14:
Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 13 and 14 have already shown why F. Qd2 stands out, but the geometry after 130...Qd2 deserves one more concrete look. From d2 the queen simultaneously maintains the second-rank perpetual net (...Qh2+/...Qg2+ after any Kh4 or Kg4), directly contests the open d-file for interpositions such as ...Qd6+ or ...Qd5+ against an e6 push, and keeps the loose Rf5 under observation so that White cannot swing the rook to f7 without allowing an immediate ...Qxf5 or a renewed series of checks.  

By contrast, L. Qc2 preserves the perpetual resource in the abstract but cedes both the d-file and pressure on the rook; after 130...Qc2 131.Kg4 the queen is one file too far left to interpose on d5/d6 in a single move, letting White reorganize the Ng3-h5-g7 battery or try Rf7 before Black re-establishes the checking sequence. The a-file waits (A, B, G, I, K, N) are already ruled out by the black a3-pawn blocking the file, and the immediate material losers (C, D, H, J, M) remain eliminated.  

Thus the single move that combines every required perpetual resource with active central control—and therefore the one that holds the draw with the least precision—is F. Qd2.
public_text.7:
Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 13 and 14 have already highlighted the decisive geometric edge that F. Qd2 holds over the rest of the second-rank options, and the latest exchanges only strengthen that case. After 130...Qd2 the queen does more than preserve the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ shuttles; it immediately eyes the loose Rf5 and keeps the d-file under direct observation. That means any attempt by White to reorganize with 131.Kg4 or 131.Kh4 can be met either by a renewed check or by ...Qd5+/...Qd6+ interpositions that gain a crucial tempo against the rook or the advancing e-pawn.  

By contrast, L. Qc2 keeps the queen on the second rank in theory but leaves the d-file open and the Rf5 untouched. After 130...Qc2 White gains an extra move to try Kg4 followed by Re5 or even Rf7 ideas before Black can re-establish the checking net, because the queen is now one file farther from the center and cannot switch to d-file resources without losing time. The pure a-file waits (A, B, G, I, K, N) suffer the same passivity once the checks run out; they preserve the perpetual in abstract but allow White greater freedom to swing the rook behind the e-pawn or reposition the knight toward f5 or e4.  

F. Qd2 therefore combines every necessary perpetual resource with the single most active central placement among the listed moves, forcing White to keep answering concrete threats rather than consolidating. That is why it emerges as the most reliable drawing continuation once the immediate losers (C, H, J, M) and the game blunder Qe6 are set aside.

public_text.5:
Colleague 6’s observation about the a3-pawn is decisive and immediately eliminates every a-file option (A, B, G, I, K, N) because those squares are now physically obstructed. That leaves only the second-rank family: E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2 and the marginal D Qf2. Among these, F Qd2 is the only square that simultaneously preserves the …Qh2+/…Qg2+ perpetual, contests the open d-file for instant interpositions against any e6 or Re5+ push, and keeps direct pressure on the loose Rf5.  

After 130…Qd2 White cannot safely try 131 e6 because …Qd6+ or …Qd3+ arrives with tempo and blocks the pawn; any attempt to swing the rook (Rf7) is met by …Qxf5 or renewed checks that force the king back. By contrast, L Qc2 cedes the d-file and leaves the Rf5 untouched, so after 131 Kg4 the queen is one file too far left to interpose on d5/d6 in a single move. This gives White a genuine window to reorganize the knight toward h5 or e4 before Black can reconnect the perpetual. The same tempo loss affects E Qb2 and D Qf2, both of which lack the d-file reach.  

Thus the geometry after 130…Qd2 forces White to keep answering concrete threats rather than consolidating, which is why it is the single most reliable drawing resource among the surviving legal moves. The game move 130…Qe6 remains the only one that hands White the decisive Kh4 tempo and the Ng3-h5-g7 net.

White’s win is e6-e7-e8 with Rf5-Ng3 battery, Rf8+/Re8+/Re5+ checks and the Kh4 Ng3-h5-g7 net. The draw is kept as long as Black can keep the queen able to return to the h-file/second rank for …Qh1+/…Qh2+/…Qg2+ perpetuals and to interpose on e6/e7 against Re5+/e6.

The a-pawn on a3 blocks the a-file upwards from a2. From a2 the queen cannot go to a3,a4,a5,a6,a7,a8. Hence B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, K Qa4, N Qa3+ and J Qa5 are illegal/losing in the actual position; J Qa5 is also losing by 131 Rxa5. The immediate material losers in the list are C Qg2+ 131 Kxg2, H Qh2+ 131 Kxh2, M Qe2 131 Nxe2 and the actually played 130…Qe6 131 Kh4 which releases the Ng3-h5-g7 net.

Once losers are removed any quiet wait which keeps the queen on a1 or on the 2nd rank keeps the …Qh2+/…Qg2+ shuttle alive and an interposition on e6/e7 available. In the list the legal drawing family is
A Qa1 – the textbook a-file retreat,
E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2
and the marginal second-rank analogue D Qf2.
e.g. 130…Qa1 131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qh4+ … and the same perpetual is obtained with 130…Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2. The same geometry is also obtainable with the checking form N Qa3+ in theory, but Qa3+ is illegal because a3 is occupied by Black’s own pawn.

F Qd2 is now the consensus most active/practical realisation of the family: from d2 the queen stays on the second rank so …Qh2+/…Qg2+ can be re-established after any Kh4/Kg4, it directly contests the open d-file for instant …Qd6+/…Qd5+ interpositions against e6/Re5+ and it eyes the loose Rf5 so White cannot swing the rook to f7 without allowing tempo loss. L Qc2, E Qb2 and D Qf2 keep the perpetual in principle but concede d-file/central pressure and give White an extra tempo to reorganise the Ng3-h5 battery. A Qa1 remains the canonical textbook citation of the same drawing idea.

Earlier over-generalisation about a-file shuttles Qa3-Qa8 is now corrected; colleagues who still invoke Qa7/Qa6/Qa8/Qa4/Qa3/Qa5 are in error given the a3 pawn. Unresolved nuance is whether D Qf2 is fully as robust as the d-file central waits; most treat it as marginal but formally retaining the second-rank perpetual. The game blunder 130…Qe6 and the immediate capturers C/H/M/J remain eliminated.
